01

Business Understanding

The ExCo is weighing three related decisions. We scope this engagement to the one that the other two sit on top of.

CEO
Return on invested capital
Wants investors funding loans through the platform to earn strong, risk-adjusted returns — which means keeping bad loans out of the funded pool.
CFO
Interest profit
Focused on the interest income Lending Club earns a cut of over the life of each loan — profit that a default erases along with the principal.
CMO
Market share vs. Prosper
Needs a durable growth story: an investor base that trusts the platform's returns is the best lever against competing marketplaces.

Underneath these three goals sit three candidate decisions: which applications to feature to investors, how to price interest rate by risk tier, and which borrower segments to prioritize for growth. We focus this analysis on the first — the screening decision — because it serves all three ExCo members at once: keeping high-risk applications out of the featured pool protects ROIC and interest profit directly, and a track record of solid investor returns is Lending Club's strongest market-share lever. Risk-based pricing and portfolio-level growth targeting both build on the same underlying risk model, and are the subject of Updates 2 and 3.

02

Source of Value

Lending Club's key asset is the historical record of funded loans and what actually happened to them. That record lets us convert experience into a screen for applications that have not funded yet.

STEP 1

Learn

Fit the statistical relationship between borrower/loan attributes known at the time of funding and the eventual default outcome, using the 9,578-loan historical sample.

→
STEP 2

Screen

Score new applications through that learned relationship before they are ever shown to investors, flagging the high-risk ones.

→
STEP 3

Improve

Fewer bad loans funded lifts ROIC and interest profit directly, and a stronger investor track record compounds into market share.

Update 1 does the groundwork for Step 1 — understanding the data and its structure — before Update 2 builds the classification models themselves.

03

Data Understanding

One row is one 3-year loan funded on the platform between May 2007 and February 2010. The critical distinction for any future model is when a field becomes known.

KNOWN AT APPLICATION — usable as predictors

credit.policypurposeint.rateinstallment log.annual.incdtificodays.with.cr.line revol.balrevol.utilinq.last.6mthsdelinq.2yrspub.rec

13 fields the investor already has in hand when deciding whether to fund the loan.

KNOWN ONLY AFTER THE OUTCOME — exclude from modeling

tot.paymentprincipalinterest

Deterministic functions of installment / int.rate and the realized outcome. Using them as predictors would leak the answer into the model — they exist only to compute profit, loss, and ROIC after a screening decision is made.

Which features should matter most for profitability? Before looking at outcomes, industry intuition points to fico (the standard repayment-risk proxy), int.rate (Lending Club's own risk assessment baked into a number), revol.util (over-leverage signal), dti (repayment capacity relative to income), inq.last.6mths (active credit-shopping / financial stress), and purpose (some stated reasons for borrowing are structurally riskier than others). Section 4 tests every one of these hypotheses against the data.

04

Descriptive Analysis

Distributions, correlation structure, and — the question that matters most — how the default rate itself moves with each variable.

4.1 · Shape of the data

Exhibit 1

purpose is dominated by debt consolidation (41%) and an "all other" catch-all (24%); 80.5% of loans pass Lending Club's own credit.policy underwriting screen.

Exhibit 2

revol.bal, dti, days.with.cr.line, and inq.last.6mths are right-skewed with long tails; delinq.2yrs and pub.rec sit at zero for most borrowers, behaving as sparse flags rather than continuous measures. fico, int.rate, and log.annual.inc are closer to bell-shaped.

4.2 · Correlation structure

Exhibit 3

As anticipated by the case: int.rate correlates strongly negative with fico (r ≈ −0.71, the single strongest pair among application-time fields — Lending Club prices risk into the rate) and positive with revol.util (utilization feeds the risk assessment behind the rate). The excluded KPI fields are, by construction, almost perfectly correlated with installment/int.rate — confirming they carry no independent information as predictors. The int.rate/fico pair motivates a variable-pruning decision in Section 5.

4.3 · Correlation structure, split by outcome

Does the co-varying structure among predictors look different for loans that defaulted vs. loans that didn't? We split the sample into defaulters (n=1,533) and non-defaulters (n=8,045) and recompute Exhibit 3 within each group.

Exhibit 3b

Application-time predictor correlations, computed separately within defaulters (left) and non-defaulters (right).

The overall shape is similar — reassuring, since it means the basic pricing/risk relationships aren't an artifact of one subgroup. But the three largest shifts all involve the same pricing/risk trio, and all move the same direction: int.rate vs. revol.util (+0.48 non-defaulters → +0.33 defaulters), fico vs. revol.util (−0.56 → −0.42), and int.rate vs. fico (−0.73 → −0.60). Lending Club's pricing signal is measurably less internally consistent among loans that went on to default — defaulters are disproportionately drawn from exactly the region where int.rate stops tracking the other risk variables cleanly. That makes a int.rate/revol.util mismatch itself worth testing as an engineered feature in Update 2. These are modest shifts (all |Δr| ≤ 0.15) on a 5:1 class imbalance, though — a hypothesis-generating result, not a final one. The more direct way to see whether combinations of variables signal risk is next.

4.4 · Where do two variables jointly signal risk?

Splitting the correlation matrix by outcome hints at which pairs might interact, but doesn't show how default rate itself moves across combinations. Instead we bin each variable into quartiles and plot the default rate directly in each 4×4 grid cell — the most direct descriptive answer to "does this combination of variables signal an especially high or low default rate?"

Exhibit 3c

Default rate (%) across quartile grids of three variable pairs, motivated by Exhibits 3 and 3b.

fico × revol.util · spread 6.9%–23.2% (16.3pp)

Within the safest FICO quartile, default rate still swings 6.9%→16.0% purely with utilization — a genuine interaction. Within the riskiest FICO quartile, utilization barely moves the needle (22–23% throughout): high utilization is already "priced in" once FICO is bad. revol.util matters most exactly where you'd be tempted to relax scrutiny.

fico × dti · spread 7.1%–24.6% (17.5pp)

Almost entirely explained by the fico axis alone — moving across dti within any FICO column changes the rate by only 1–5 points, no consistent direction. A useful negative result: no interaction here worth engineering.

revol.util × inq.last.6mths · spread 8.5%–28.6% (20.1pp, widest)

Both variables add signal independently. The single riskiest cell of all three grids: utilization 46–71% combined with 2+ recent inquiries → 28.6% default (n=521) — a concrete, testable screening rule for Update 2.

So, is the split-correlation-matrix approach the right one? On its own, not really — two-variable default-rate grids like Exhibit 3c are the more direct way to answer "does this combination signal high or low risk," since they show the effect in the actual units that matter (default rate) and make plain when an interaction exists (revol.util × inq.last.6mths, and revol.util conditional on high fico) versus when it's really just one variable in disguise (fico × dti). The split correlation matrices (Exhibit 3b) remain useful as a first-pass, correlation-only scan across all 12 predictors at once, to flag which pairs are worth a bivariate grid — the two techniques work best as a pair.

4.5 · How default rate actually moves

100%-normalized views, so the red band height reads directly as the default rate for that bucket.

Exhibit 4

Default rate against octiles of fico, int.rate, revol.util, inq.last.6mths, dti, and log.annual.inc.

Exhibit 5

Default rate by purpose and by credit.policy.

dti and log.annual.inc are comparatively flat, with only a mild uptick in the riskiest extreme bin — weaker standalone predictors than the six above. These findings confirm the Section 3 hypotheses and set the variable list for clustering and PCA below.

05

K-Means Clustering

Clustering uses the co-varying patterns among borrower attributes to find naturally occurring segments — independent of the default label itself.

Scope constraint. Every variable considered for clustering (and for the PCA in Section 06) is known at the time of the funding decision — no exceptions. default, tot.payment, principal, and interest are never used as inputs anywhere below.

Variables. Starting point: eight scaled, continuous, application-time numeric fields — installment, log.annual.inc, dti, fico, days.with.cr.line, revol.bal, revol.util, inq.last.6mths. We exclude credit.policy (a binary flag downstream of the others), and delinq.2yrs/pub.rec (Exhibit 2 — overwhelmingly zero, near-zero variance that would just add noise to a distance-based method).

Correlation-based pruning

Why int.rate is dropped from clustering & PCA

int.rate vs. fico (r ≈ −0.71) is the single strongest correlation among all application-time numeric fields — well above the next-strongest pair (fico vs. revol.util, r ≈ −0.54, Exhibit 3). Keeping both in a Euclidean-distance method would double-weight the same underlying risk signal, so we keep fico and drop int.rate:

  • fico is a primitive, exogenous borrower attribute (a credit-bureau score); int.rate is Lending Club's own derived output — a decision the platform already made using fico plus other risk factors. Clustering on it risks rediscovering Lending Club's existing pricing tiers rather than revealing independent structure.
  • Dropping it frees int.rate up as an external check: if the clusters we find — built with zero pricing information — still line up with Lending Club's own rates and with realized default rates, that's stronger evidence the segments are real. Anywhere they don't line up is a potential pricing blind spot.

Final variable set (8 variables, all known at application): installment, log.annual.inc, dti, fico, days.with.cr.line, revol.bal, revol.util, inq.last.6mths.

Exhibit 6

Elbow (inertia) and silhouette score across k = 2–8, on the 8-variable set. Both curves are flat, with silhouette peaking mildly at k=2–3.

Exhibit 7

Standardized cluster centers across all eight clustering variables, used to name each segment.

With int.rate removed, both curves are, if anything, flatter than before — typical of real borrower data with overlapping, continuous risk gradients rather than tight natural clusters. We keep k = 4: it costs little silhouette quality relative to k = 2/3 while separating out the small, high-balance outlier segment and producing named, actionable archetypes for the ExCo.

CLUSTER 3

High-FICO, low-utilization safe borrowers

9.2%default
2,837 loans · 30% of book
Highest fico (~751), lowest dti (~8.3), lowest revol.util (~19%), fewest inq.last.6mths; 95% pass credit.policy. Lowest int.rate too (10.05%, not a clustering input) — Lending Club's own pricing agrees this is the safe segment.
CLUSTER 1

Short-history, small-loan borrowers

18.9%default
3,785 loans · 40% of book — largest segment
Smallest loans (installment ~$202), lowest income, shortest credit history (~3,110 days), lowest fico (~689).
CLUSTER 2

High-utilization revolvers

18.3%default
2,768 loans · 29% of book
Largest installments among the "typical" clusters (~$474), highest revol.util (~67%), above-average income, below-average fico. Highest int.rate on average (13.54%).
CLUSTER 0

High-income jumbo revolvers

28.2%default
188 loans · 2% of book — small outlier segment
Extreme revol.bal (mean ~$190.8k, z ≈ +5.2), highest income, longest credit history, highest dti — yet only 20% pass credit.policy, and default the most of any segment (28.2%).
New finding · pricing gap

Lending Club's own rates don't fully track realized risk across these segments

Ranking clusters by average int.rate gives 3 < 1 < 0 < 2 (Cluster 2 is priced highest on average). Ranking the same clusters by realized default rate gives 3 < 2 < 1 < 0 (Cluster 0 defaults most). Cluster 0 — the high-income jumbo-revolver outlier, just 2% of volume — has the worst default rate in the book (28.2%) yet is priced below Cluster 2 (13.01% vs. 13.54%). That's a concrete, testable pricing blind spot: a small but disproportionately risky segment that current rate-setting does not appear to price high enough relative to its actual loss experience.

What this buys us for modeling. A natural, unsupervised risk stratification built with zero pricing information — useful to sanity-check that a later logistic regression / tree model's predicted risk ranks track these segments, and now directly comparable against Lending Club's own pricing. The Cluster 0 pricing gap above is a concrete lead for Update 2: test whether a revol.bal-driven flag (or cluster membership itself) adds predictive power for default beyond what int.rate already captures. Cluster 1, the largest segment at 40% of volume and above-average risk, is a natural target for tighter screening rules and for the CMO's growth strategy. Segment membership itself could become an engineered categorical feature for Update 2's classification models — and, because int.rate was never an input, it would add information genuinely independent of Lending Club's current pricing rather than partly re-deriving it.

06

Principal Component Analysis

A complementary, continuous view to K-means: weighted combinations of the same eight application-time variables that capture the directions of highest variability among loans — again with no pricing information and no outcome label as inputs.

Exhibit 8

PC1 + PC2 explain ~48% of variance; 7 of 8 components are needed to reach 90% — variance is spread fairly evenly across the eight attributes.

Exhibit 9

Variable loadings across all eight components.

PC1 · 24.8% of variance

Scale / establishment axis

log.annual.inc+0.56
revol.bal+0.48
installment+0.48
days.with.cr.line+0.42

High PC1 = higher income, larger absolute revolving balance, bigger installment, longer credit history — a larger, more established borrower. fico loads almost at zero (+0.09): with int.rate removed, PC1 is now a near-pure scale axis with almost no risk signal in it — cleaner than a first pass where int.rate's dominant loading pulled a risk flavor into PC1.

PC2 · 23.1% of variance · cumulative 47.9%

Safety axis

fico+0.61
revol.util−0.59
dti−0.43

High PC2 = higher FICO, lower revolving utilization, lower debt-to-income — a safer borrower (the same three variables Exhibit 3 flagged as int.rate's closest substitutes, now doing the work on their own). PC3 (13.0%, not pictured) is dominated almost entirely by inq.last.6mths (+0.88) — a near single-variable "credit-shopping intensity" component.

Exhibit 10

Biplot of PC1 (scale) vs. PC2 (safety), points colored by cluster (the four K-means segments from Section 05), with variable loading vectors overlaid. Neither int.rate nor default was used to build this plot.

Cluster ↔ PCA cross-check

The four K-means segments land in distinct regions of the plane

Coloring the same points by K-means cluster instead of by default gives a direct, visual check of whether the two unsupervised methods agree — even more cleanly than with int.rate included.

Cluster Mean PC1 Mean PC2 Reading
3 — High-FICO, low-utilization safe borrowers −0.07 +1.63 Stands apart almost entirely on the safety axis, near-average on scale — exactly as named.
1 — Short-history, small-loan borrowers −1.00 −0.73 Lowest scale score — smallest loans, shortest history, lowest income — and below-average safety.
2 — High-utilization revolvers 1.13 −0.63 Above-average scale, below-average safety — similar safety to Cluster 1 but larger loans.
0 — High-income jumbo revolvers 4.45 −0.69 The clear scale outlier, consistent with its extreme revol.bal — with below-average safety on top of that.

The structure is remarkably clean: PC2 alone separates the safe cluster (3) from the other three, which all sit at similar, below-average safety (−0.6 to −0.7); PC1 then separates those other three by scale (jumbo revolvers > high-utilization revolvers > short-history small-loan borrowers). Two independently fitted unsupervised methods — K-means on 8 raw scaled features, PCA on the same 8 features, neither given int.rate or default — recover the same underlying structure, which is exactly the kind of convergence that makes this variable shortlist defensible to the ExCo.

Reading the extremes

Highest PC1 (largest / most established — Cluster 0)

installment $831.52, revol.bal at the data's maximum ($1,207,359), high income, fico 717, a small_business loan that fails credit.policy — exactly the extreme-scale profile PC1 is built to flag. int.rate was 14.96% (not a PCA input). Outcome: defaulted

Lowest PC1 (smallest / least established — Cluster 1)

installment $15.91 — essentially the smallest loan in the data — near-zero reported income (log 7.60, ≈ $2,000/yr, a likely data-quality flag), zero revolving balance, decent fico (702). Despite the healthy FICO: Outcome: defaulted — a reminder PC1 (scale) says nothing about safety on its own.

Highest PC2 (safest profile — Cluster 3)

fico 812 (near the data's maximum), revol.util 0.3%, dti 0.22, zero inquiries — a textbook ultra-safe borrower. int.rate was 7.12%, the lowest of any example here. Outcome: paid in full

Lowest PC2 (riskiest-looking profile — Cluster 0)

fico 672, revol.util 99%, dti 14.39, revol.bal ≈ $952k — and Lending Club evidently agreed: int.rate was 20.11%, the highest of any example here. Yet: Outcome: paid in full — PC2, like PC1, describes a risk tendency in the population, not a certainty for any one loan.

What this buys us for modeling. PC2 is a ready-made, single-number safety score built purely from unsupervised structure with no pricing information at all — a useful baseline against the logistic regression coefficients we will estimate in Update 2 (do fico, revol.util, and dti dominate there too?). Near-orthogonality of PC1 and PC2 suggests scale and safety are two largely independent dimensions worth retaining separately; removing int.rate made this separation noticeably cleaner than in a first pass where its dominant loading blurred a risk flavor into PC1. The Cluster 0 pricing gap from Section 05 is visible here too: Cluster 0 sits at below-average PC2 alongside Clusters 1 and 2, yet its realized default rate is meaningfully worse than either — worth carrying into Update 2 as a specific hypothesis to test with a supervised model.

Update 1 · Summary for the ExCo

Three independent lenses, zero pricing information, one convergent structure

Correlation analysis, K-means clustering, and PCA were run independently on the same eight application-time variables — deliberately excluding int.rate and default from the unsupervised methods — and all three still converge on the same core structure. That convergence, built with no pricing information at all, is what makes this variable shortlist defensible to carry into Update 2's classification models.

ficorevol.utildtiinq.last.6mthslog.annual.increvol.balpurposecredit.policy
Correlation & default-rate analysis

Default rate moves 3–4x across the range of fico, int.rate, revol.util, and inq.last.6mths. int.rate vs. fico (r ≈ −0.71) is the standout correlation — the basis for excluding int.rate from clustering/PCA.

K-means (4 segments, no int.rate)

Safe high-FICO borrowers (30%, 9.2% default) at one end, high-income jumbo revolvers (2%, 28.2% default) at the other. New: the jumbo-revolver segment defaults most but is priced below the high-utilization-revolver segment — a pricing gap.

PCA (2 axes, 48% variance, no int.rate)

A scale/establishment axis (PC1) and an orthogonal safety axis (PC2, fico/revol.util/dti) — cleaner than a first pass with int.rate included, and the same four clusters visibly separate along it.

Bridge to Update 2 — this shortlist, the four K-means segments as a candidate engineered feature, and the Cluster 0 pricing-gap hypothesis all carry forward into the logistic regression and decision-tree default models next. tot.payment, principal, and interest remain excluded throughout, reserved for computing profit, loss, and ROIC once a screening threshold is chosen in Update 3; int.rate re-enters in Update 2 as a candidate predictor in its own right (supervised methods can handle correlated predictors quite differently from Euclidean-distance clustering), evaluated there alongside — not instead of — the borrower attributes it is itself derived from.
